content.text: Base directory for this skill: /Users/rohinibarla/src/github.com/aikaryashala/jun-2026/.claude/skills/create-task # Create a worksheet task This project is a static educational site under `docs/` for beginner students who are **Telugu speakers learning in English**, mostly running an **Ubuntu VM over Windows WSL**. Each task teaches one topic through a worksheet, a question bank, and an answer key, each rendered by a slim HTML viewer. Full conventions live in the repo root **`CLAUDE.md`** — read it before starting. ## The workflow (do these in order) ### 1. Understand the topic From the discussion or the "create task on " request, pin down: - the single concept and the concrete skill the student should walk away with; - which earlier tasks it builds on (skim `docs/tasks.html` for the sequence); - whether it is **C-code + debugger** based, **shell** based, or a **tools/reference** task (some tasks — e.g. task12 images, task13 command checklist — are not the full six-file shape); - any **staged vocabulary** the user is deliberately withholding (e.g. the word "pointer" was introduced only in later tasks; "address variable" was used first). Respect it — never introduce a term the user is saving for later. ### 2. Pick the task number and base name - Next number = highest existing `docs/taskN/` + 1. - `` is snake_case and shared by all files (e.g. `bitwise_operators`, `address_variables`). Worksheet file is `_worksheet.md`. ### 3. Propose an outline — THIS IS THE REVIEW GATE Do **not** create any files yet. Present a written outline and ask the user to review and discuss it. Include: - **Task number, title, and base filename.** - **Worksheet**: the "golden rule" blockquote idea; the ordered list of iterations, each as a one-line idea plus what the student *sets up* and *observes*; any C programs to be written; the practice set; the reference-table topics; and a note that a Telugu "New Words" table will close it. If the topic suits discovery-first teaching, offer that structure (observe sample(s) → student forms a theory → then the explanation) as an option. - **Questions**: the parts (e.g. A = MCQ, B = fill-in-the-blanks, C = scenarios / trace) and rough counts, plus the kinds of items. Note that questions reveal no answers and that **titles must not give away what to observe**. - **Answers**: mirrors the question numbering, every answer with reasoning, closing "pattern to notice" note. - **What will be verified** (programs compiled, arithmetic/traces checked). Then explicitly invite review: the user may change scope, iterations, examples, counts, terminology, or pedagogy. **Iterate on the outline until the user clearly confirms.** Only a clear go-ahead ("yes", "create it", "confirmed") unlocks step 4. ### 4. On confirmation — create the files Create under `docs/taskN/`: - `_worksheet.md`, `_questions.md`, `_answers.md` following the formats in `CLAUDE.md` (a/b/c iterations + "Takeaway to say out loud"; one-page reference; New Words table; question parts; reasoned answers). - **Verify everything first.** Compile and run every C program and every trace in the scratchpad; check all arithmetic by hand. In sample debugger transcripts use **Linux/WSL-style** addresses (`0x00007fffffff...`, `libc` frames), never the macOS values this machine prints. Do **not** rely on this machine's stack layout for answers — for question snippets that must be portable, use address variables into **arrays** (element layout is guaranteed) so answers match the students' Ubuntu exactly. Keep any deliberate design constraint (e.g. "int only") silent — it shapes the examples but is never announced to students. - Create the three viewers by copying the most recent slim viewer of each kind (e.g. from `docs/task14/`) and changing **only**: ``, `<body class>` (`worksheet`/`questions`/`answers`), `.brand` text, the topbar stage chips, and the status-line text. Everything else comes from `docs/assets/viewer.css` and `docs/assets/viewer.js`. **A viewer's `.html` basename must exactly equal its `.md` basename** (the shared JS derives the markdown filename from the page URL). - **Update `docs/tasks.html`**: add one `<li>` to the `.tasklist` of whichever topic group the task belongs to (`#linux`, `#c`, `#memory`, `#debug`, `#tools`, `#python`), in task-number order within that group — ```html <li><span class="num">Task N</span> <a class="title" href="taskN/<base>_worksheet.html"><Title></a> <a class="q" href="taskN/<base>_questions.html">Questions</a> <a class="q" href="taskN/<base>_answers.html">ans</a></li> ``` (For a tool/reference task with no question bank, replace the two `.q` links with `<span class="only">worksheet only</span>` or `<span class="only">reference</span>`. Use `Extra Questions`/`extra ans` for an `_extra_` bank.) - **Update `docs/index.html`**: add the number to that group's path chip (e.g. `tasks 3, 5, 7`), bump the worksheet count in `.facts`, and — if the batch is moving on to this task — update the `WHERE WE ARE NOW` block. Both spots are marked with comments in the file. ### 5. Verify and report - Serve `docs/` (`python3 -m http.server`) and confirm every new page and its markdown return 200; confirm each viewer's derived markdown exists. - Report what was created: the files, the worksheet's iterations, the question counts, and confirmation that programs/answers were verified. ## Guardrails - **Never create files before the user confirms the outline** (step 3). - One new idea per iteration; predict-before-reveal; the New Words Telugu table is always the last worksheet section. - Don't announce design constraints to students; don't introduce staged vocabulary early. - Verify by running, not by assuming; keep transcripts Ubuntu/WSL-accurate. - Match the file/viewer conventions exactly so the shared assets keep working. ARGUMENTS: as task22 for the topic on 'Pull Request', Cover all the fundamentals regarding Pull Request.
I'll start by reading the project conventions and looking at the existing Git task (task21) since this builds directly on it.

The page kind comes from the body class: 49 - `` → `hr` divider mark `›`, plus worksheet-only table rules 50 (first column nowrap, last column wraps for Telugu) 51 - `` → divider mark `?` 52 - `` → divider mark `✓` 53 - **`viewer.js`** — fetches the page's markdown and renders it with marked.js + 54 highlight.js (only fences with a known language tag get highlighted; ASCII diagrams 55 use plain fences). **No per-page config:** the markdown name is derived from the page 56 URL (`.html` → `.md`), so a viewer's `.html` basename MUST exactly equal 57 its `.md` basename. Error wording comes from the body class. The `file://` fallback 58 tells students to serve the `docs` folder (serving a task folder alone would 404 59 `../assets/`). 60 61 A viewer page contains only: ``, font + highlight-theme links, the 62 `../assets/viewer.css` link, the topbar (`.brand` text + stage chips), the status line 63 ("Rendering worksheet…/questions…/answers…"), the marked/hljs CDN scripts, and 64 `../assets/viewer.js`. 65 66 **Creating a new viewer:** copy any existing slim viewer and change only: `<title>`, 67 body class, brand text, chips, status-line text. Nothing else. 68 69 **Legacy exceptions (leave alone):** `task3/relative-vs-absolute-paths.html` and 70 `task3/relative-vs-absolute-paths-key.html` are an older standalone design with their 71 own inline CSS/JS; they are not on the shared assets. Task3's question-bank answer key 72 is named `-questions-answers.*` because a worksheet-level `-answers.md` already existed. 73 74 ## Content formats 75 76 - **Worksheet:** `# Title`, goal + what's needed, a "golden rule/picture" blockquote, 77 iterations separated by `---`, each with `**a. What we set up**`, `**b. Task**`, 78 `**c. Observation (what you should find)**`, and `**Takeaway to say out loud:**`; 79 then practice with self-check, a one-page reference table, and always last: 80 `## New Words (కొత్త పదాలు — తెలుగు అర్థాలు)` (English | తెలుగు | simple meaning). 81 - **Question bank** (`_questions.md`): Part A Multiple Choice (~12–14, options A–D), 82 Part B Fill in the Blanks (~10), Part C Scenario Questions (~8). Questions only — 83 never any answers in this file. Question titles may name a scenario but must never 84 reveal what the student should observe. 85 - **Answer key** (`_answers.md`): mirrors the numbering; every answer explains the 86 *why* (line-by-line traces where applicable); tell students to check the reasoning, 87 not just the letter. 88 - Design constraints (e.g. "int only" in task8) are author-side: they shape the 89 examples silently and are never announced to students. 90 - Verify every claim by hand before shipping: arithmetic, source line numbers referred 91 to by debugger output, expected program output. Students run on a Linux VM 92 (WSL on Windows) — use Linux-style paths/addresses in sample transcripts, not macOS. 93 94 ## The hub pages (index.html, tasks.html, slides) 95 96 Three hand-written pages — not viewers — sharing `assets/site.css`, which reuses the 97 same tokens as `viewer.css` so the front door looks like the worksheets: 98 99 - **`index.html`** — the batch landing page served at the site root. Hero (batch label, 100 student/team/worksheet counts), a **"Now on"** banner naming the task the batch is 101 currently working through, a **learning path** of topic chips linking to `tasks.html` 102 anchors, and three hub cards. Two things go stale and are marked with comments in the 103 file: the `BRANDING` lines and the `WHERE WE ARE NOW` block — update the "Now on" 104 link whenever the batch moves to a new task. 105 - **`tasks.html`** — the worksheet index (this was the old `index.html`; renamed 106 2026-08-06 so the root could become the batch page). The task number lives in its 112 own `.num` span, so the link text is the title alone (no "Task N -" prefix): 113 114 ```html 115 <li><span class="num">Task N</span> 116 <a class="title" href="taskN/<base>.html"><Title></a> 117 <a class="q" href="taskN/<base>_questions.html">Questions</a> 118 <a class="q" href="taskN/<base>_answers.html">ans</a></li> 119 ``` 120 121 For a worksheet-only or reference task, replace the two `.q` links with 122 `<span class="only">worksheet only</span>` (or `reference`). 123 124 ## Serving locally 125 126 Viewers `fetch()` their sibling `.md`, so `file://` won't work. 1	# Git Internals — Inside the `.git` Folder
2	
3	**Goal.** You have used `git add` and `git commit` before. Today you will open the box. You will see exactly which files `git init` creates, where your name and email are stored, watch objects appear inside `.git/objects/` one by one as you commit, and then write **hooks** — small scripts Git runs for you at fixed moments, including one that refuses a bad commit.
4	
5	**You need:** your Linux VM (WSL), a terminal, `git`, a notebook, and a pencil.
6	
7	Check Git is there:
8	
9	```
10	git --version
11	```
12	
13	You should see something like `git version 2.43.0`. Any `2.x` is fine; a few file names differ slightly between versions, and the worksheet says so where it matters.
14	
15	Make a folder for today:
16	
17	```
18	mkdir -p ~/task21
19	cd ~/task21
20	```
21	
22	> **The golden rule of Git**
23	> `.git` is not magic and it is not a black box — it is a folder of ordinary files. Every version of every file you commit is saved there as an **object**, and each object's name is a **hash of its own contents**. Everything else — branches, `HEAD`, the staging area — is just a small file holding one of those names.
24	
25	*(A note on paths: everything today happens inside your own `~/task21` folder. Nothing here touches the internet, and nothing here can damage another repository.)*
26	
27	---
28	
29	## Iteration 1 — What `git init` actually creates
30	
31	**a. What we set up**
32	
33	Nothing yet. Just an empty folder and one command.
34	
35	**b. Task**
36	
37	Before running, write down your guess: how many files and folders does `git init` create? One? Five? Twenty?
38	
39	```
40	cd ~/task21
41	git init demo
42	cd demo
43	ls -a
44	```
45	
46	Then look inside:
47	
48	```
49	find .git | sort
50	```
51	
52	**c. Observation (what you should find)**
53	
54	The `git init` command says this:
55	
56	```
57	hint: Using 'master' as the name for the initial branch. This default branch name
58	hint: is subject to change. To configure the initial branch name to use in all
59	hint: of your new repositories, which will suppress this warning, call:
60	hint:
61	hint: 	git config --global init.defaultBranch <name>
62	hint:
63	hint: Names commonly chosen instead of 'master' are 'main', 'trunk' and
64	hint: 'development'. The just-created branch can be renamed via this command:
65	hint:
66	hint: 	git branch -m <name>
67	Initialized empty Git repository in /home/student/task21/demo/.git/
68	```
69	
70	Keep that hint in mind — Iteration 2 will make it disappear.
71	
72	`ls -a` shows only one new thing:
73	
74	```
75	.  ..  .git
76	```
77	
78	**Everything Git knows lives inside that one folder.** Delete `.git` and you have an ordinary folder of files again, with no history.
79	
80	`find .git | sort` shows what is inside:
81	
82	```
83	.git
84	.git/HEAD
85	.git/branches
86	.git/config
87	.git/description
88	.git/hooks
89	.git/hooks/applypatch-msg.sample
90	.git/hooks/commit-msg.sample
91	.git/hooks/fsmonitor-watchman.sample
92	.git/hooks/post-update.sample
93	.git/hooks/pre-applypatch.sample
94	.git/hooks/pre-commit.sample
95	.git/hooks/pre-merge-commit.sample
96	.git/hooks/pre-push.sample
97	.git/hooks/pre-rebase.sample
98	.git/hooks/pre-receive.sample
99	.git/hooks/prepare-commit-msg.sample
100	.git/hooks/push-to-checkout.sample
101	.git/hooks/sendemail-validate.sample
102	.git/hooks/update.sample
103	.git/info
104	.git/info/exclude
105	.git/objects
106	.git/objects/info
107	.git/objects/pack
108	.git/refs
109	.git/refs/heads
110	.git/refs/tags
111	```
112	
113	*(The exact list of `.sample` files varies a little between Git versions, and `branches/` is gone in Git 2.45 and newer. Do not memorise the list — memorise the four important entries below.)*
114	
115	Here is what matters:
116	
117	| Entry | What it is |
118	|---|---|
119	| `HEAD` | a **text file** saying which branch you are on |
120	| `config` | this repository's own settings |
121	| `objects/` | where every version of every file will be stored — **empty right now** |
122	| `refs/heads/` | one small file per branch — **empty right now** |
123	| `hooks/` | scripts Git will run at fixed moments (Iteration 6) |
124	| `description` | only used by an old web tool; ignore it |
125	| `info/exclude` | like `.gitignore`, but private to you and not committed |
126	
127	Now read `HEAD` — it really is just text:
128	
129	```
130	cat .git/HEAD
131	```
132	```
133	ref: refs/heads/master
134	```
135	
136	It points at `refs/heads/master`. But look again at the `find` output: **there is no file `refs/heads/master`.** `HEAD` is pointing at a branch that does not exist yet. That is exactly what "no commits yet" means.
137	
138	And `config`:
139	
140	```
141	cat .git/config
142	```
143	```
144	[core]
145		repositoryformatversion = 0
146		filemode = true
147		bare = false
148		logallrefupdates = true
149	```
150	
151	Four lines. No name, no email — Git has not saved anything about *you* here.
152	
153	Two more things are **not** there yet. Check:
154	
155	```
156	ls .git/index
157	find .git/objects -type f | wc -l
158	find .git/refs -type f | wc -l
159	```
160	```
161	ls: cannot access '.git/index': No such file or directory
162	0
163	0
164	```
165	
166	No staging area, no objects, no branches. A fresh repository is almost entirely empty.
167	
168	**Takeaway to say out loud:** "`git init` makes one folder, `.git`, and it starts out nearly empty — no objects, no branches, not even an index."
169	
170	---
171	
172	## Iteration 2 — Where your settings are stored
173	
174	Git needs to know your name and email to record a commit. Where does it keep them?
175	
176	**a. What we set up**
177	
178	Git reads settings from **three files**, in this order:
179	
180	| Level | File | Applies to |
181	|---|---|---|
182	| system | `/etc/gitconfig` | every user on the machine |
183	| **global** | `~/.gitconfig` | **you**, in every repository |
184	| local | `.git/config` | this one repository only |
185	
186	Later beats earlier: **local wins over global, and global wins over system.**
187	
188	**b. Task**
189	
190	First check whether the system file even exists, and what Git can see right now:
191	
192	```
193	ls -l /etc/gitconfig
194	git config --list --show-origin
195	```
196	
197	Then set your identity globally, and find the file it wrote:
198	
199	```
200	git config --global user.name "Ravi Kumar"
201	git config --global user.email "ravi@example.com"
202	git config --global init.defaultBranch main
203	
204	ls -a ~ | grep gitconfig
205	cat ~/.gitconfig
206	```
207	
208	*(Use your **own** name and email, not Ravi's.)*
209	
210	**c. Observation (what you should find)**
211	
212	On Ubuntu there is usually no system file at all:
213	
214	```
215	ls: cannot access '/etc/gitconfig': No such file or directory
216	```
217	
218	and before you set anything, `--show-origin` lists only the repository's own four settings:
219	
220	```
221	file:.git/config	core.repositoryformatversion=0
222	file:.git/config	core.filemode=true
223	file:.git/config	core.bare=false
224	file:.git/config	core.logallrefupdates=true
225	```
226	
227	After the three `--global` commands, a new file has appeared **in your home folder** — not in the project:
228	
229	```
230	.gitconfig
231	```
232	```
233	[user]
234		name = Ravi Kumar
235		email = ravi@example.com
236	[init]
237		defaultBranch = main
238	```
239	
240	That is all `--global` means: *write it to `~/.gitconfig`.* It is an ordinary text file you could have typed yourself.
241	
242	Now `--show-origin` names the file each setting came from:
243	
244	```
245	file:/home/student/.gitconfig	user.name=Ravi Kumar
246	file:/home/student/.gitconfig	user.email=ravi@example.com
247	file:/home/student/.gitconfig	init.defaultbranch=main
248	file:.git/config	core.repositoryformatversion=0
249	file:.git/config	core.filemode=true
250	file:.git/config	core.bare=false
251	file:.git/config	core.logallrefupdates=true
252	```
253	
254	**Now prove that local wins.** Set a different email *without* `--global`:
255	
256	```
257	git config user.email "ravi@school.edu"
258	cat .git/config
259	```
260	```
261	[core]
262		repositoryformatversion = 0
263		filemode = true
264		bare = false
265		logallrefupdates = true
266	[user]
267		email = ravi@school.edu
268	```
269	
270	It went into `.git/config`, the repository's own file. Which one does Git actually use?
271	
272	```
273	git config user.email
274	git config --show-origin user.email
275	git config --global user.email
276	```
277	```
278	ravi@school.edu
279	file:.git/config	ravi@school.edu
280	ravi@example.com
281	```
282	
283	The local one wins here, and the global one is untouched — it still applies everywhere else. Remove the local override and the global comes back:
284	
285	```
286	git config --unset user.email
287	git config user.email
288	```
289	```
290	ravi@example.com
291	```
292	
293	Finally, start a fresh repository and watch the hint disappear, because `init.defaultBranch` is now set:
294	
295	```
296	cd ~/task21
297	rm -rf demo
298	git init demo
299	cd demo
300	cat .git/HEAD
301	```
302	```
303	Initialized empty Git repository in /home/student/task21/demo/.git/
304	ref: refs/heads/main
305	```
306	
307	No hint, and the branch is `main`. **Keep this new `demo` folder — the rest of the worksheet uses it.**
308	
309	**Takeaway to say out loud:** "`--global` just writes to `~/.gitconfig`; the repo's own `.git/config` beats it."
310	
311	---
312	
313	## Iteration 3 — The first object appears (and it is not at commit time)
314	
315	**a. What we set up**
316	
317	One small file, in the `demo` folder from Iteration 2:
318	
319	```
320	cd ~/task21/demo
321	printf 'hello\n' > hello.txt
322	```
323	
324	Git names every object by a **hash** of its contents — a long hex string worked out from the bytes themselves. You can ask for that hash *before* Git stores anything:
325	
326	```
327	git hash-object hello.txt
328	```
329	
330	**b. Task**
331	
332	Predict: does `git hash-object` create anything inside `.git/objects/`? Then check the count before and after each step below.
333	
334	```
335	git hash-object hello.txt
336	find .git/objects -type f | wc -l
337	
338	git add hello.txt
339	find .git/objects -type f
340	```
341	
342	**c. Observation (what you should find)**
343	
344	```
345	ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a
346	0
347	```
348	
349	`hash-object` only *calculates* — it stores nothing. Still zero objects.
350	
351	Then `git add`:
352	
353	```

641	fsmonitor-watchman.sample
642	post-update.sample

662	 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
663	 create mode 100644 a.txt

669	
670	```sh

672	if git diff --cached --name-only | grep -q "secret"; then
673	    echo "BLOCKED: a file name contains 'secret'"
674	    exit 1
675	fi
676	exit 0

711	**a. What we set up**

714	
715	```

717	rm secret_key.txt
718	rm .git/hooks/pre-commit
719	```
720	
721	Now four hooks that each announce themselves.
722	
723	Then create all four, each containing its own name:
724	
725	```sh
726	#!/bin/sh
727	echo "   >> pre-commit ran"
728	exit 0
729	```
730	
731	…and the same for `prepare-commit-msg`, `commit-msg`, and `post-commit`. Remember `chmod +x` on all four.
732	
733	**b. Task**
734	
735	Predict the **order** they will print in. Then:
736	
737	```
738	printf 'z\n' > order.txt
739	git add order.txt
740	git commit -m "Order test"
741	```
742	
743	**c. Observation (what you should find)**
744	
745	```
746	   >> pre-commit ran
747	   >> prepare-commit-msg ran
748	   >> commit-msg ran
749	   >> post-commit ran
750	[main 3e48745] Order test
751	 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
752	 create mode 100644 order.txt
753	```
754	
755	The order, and what each moment is for:
756	
757	| Hook | Fires | Good for | Can it block? |
758	|---|---|---|---|
759	| `pre-commit` | before the message is even asked for | checking the **code**: formatting, linting, secrets | **yes** |
760	| `prepare-commit-msg` | after the default message is written, before you edit it | **filling in** a message template | yes (rarely used to) |
761	| `commit-msg` | after the message is final | checking the **message** | **yes** |
762	| `post-commit` | after the commit exists | notifying, logging | **no** — too late |
763	
764	**`commit-msg` is handed the message.** Git passes it the path to a file containing what you typed, as `$1`. Replace the `commit-msg` hook with one that enforces a house style:
765	
766	```sh
767	#!/bin/sh
768	echo "   >> commit-msg received: $1"
769	echo "   >> first line: $(head -1 "$1")"
770	if ! head -1 "$1" | grep -qE '^(feat|fix|docs): '; then
771	    echo "   BLOCKED: message must start with feat:, fix: or docs:"
772	    exit 1
773	fi
774	exit 0
775	```
776	
777	```
778	printf 'y\n' > msg.txt
779	git add msg.txt
780	git commit -m "changed some stuff"
781	```
782	```
783	   >> pre-commit ran
784	   >> prepare-commit-msg ran
785	   >> commit-msg received: .git/COMMIT_EDITMSG
786	   >> first line: changed some stuff
787	   BLOCKED: message must start with feat:, fix: or docs:
788	```
789	
790	The message lives in `.git/COMMIT_EDITMSG` — a file you saw appear back in Iteration 4. Note that **`post-commit` did not run**: the commit was cancelled, so there was nothing to run after. Now with a good message:
791	
792	```
793	git commit -m "feat: add msg file"
794	```
795	```
796	   >> pre-commit ran
797	   >> prepare-commit-msg ran
798	   >> commit-msg received: .git/COMMIT_EDITMSG
799	   >> first line: feat: add msg file
800	   >> post-commit ran
801	[main 00f7378] feat: add msg file
802	 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
803	 create mode 100644 msg.txt
804	```
805	
806	All four run, and the commit is made.
807	
808	**One escape hatch.** `--no-verify` skips `pre-commit` and `commit-msg` entirely:
809	
810	```

812	```
813	
814	So hooks are a **helpful guard, not a security wall** — anyone with the repository can bypass them. This is exactly why the serious checks also run on the server, which is Iteration 8.
815	
816	**Takeaway to say out loud:** "`pre-commit` checks the code, `commit-msg` checks the message, `post-commit` is too late to stop anything."

866	```

868	```

871	
872	```

874	remote: [server] REJECTED: main is protected, open a pull request

881	
882	`pre-receive` reads three values per line — the old hash, the new hash, and the ref being updated — which is how it knows a push targets `refs/heads/main`. Push a different branch and it is allowed:
883	
884	```
885	git switch -c feature-login
886	printf 'login\n' > login.txt

893	To /home/student/task21/server.git

895	```

904	echo "[local] a test failed!"

913	[local] a test failed!

915	```

918

920

937	## Iteration 9 — How hooks are really used, and why you never see them
938	
939	**a. What we set up**
940	
941	No commands. Look back at the hooks you wrote and match each to a real job.
942	
943	**b. Task**
944	
945	Before reading on, answer one puzzle in your notebook. You have written five hooks today. Run:
946	
947	```
948	cd ~/task21/demo
949	git switch main
950	git status --short
951	git ls-files
952	```
953	
954	Your teammate clones this repository tomorrow. **Do they get your hooks?** Why or why not?
955	
956	**c. Observation (what you should find)**
957	
958	```
959	a.txt
960	hello.txt
961	msg.txt
962	notes/day1.txt
963	order.txt
964	```
965	
966	`git status --short` prints nothing at all, and your hooks are nowhere in `git ls-files`. **Hooks live inside `.git/`, and Git never tracks its own folder.** So they are not committed, not pushed, and not cloned. Your teammate gets none of them.
967	
968	That is a deliberate safety decision: cloning a repository must never run someone else's scripts on your machine. But it leaves teams with a real problem — how do you give everyone the same `pre-commit` check? Two standard answers:
969	
970	- **`core.hooksPath`** — a setting that points Git at a *tracked* folder instead. Commit your scripts to `.githooks/`, and each person runs `git config core.hooksPath .githooks` once.
971	- **The `pre-commit` framework** — a widely used tool (`pip install pre-commit`). The team commits a `.pre-commit-config.yaml` file listing the checks; each person runs `pre-commit install` once, which writes the real hook into `.git/hooks/` for them.
972	
973	Both work the same way underneath: the hook file still has to end up in `.git/hooks/`, or `core.hooksPath` has to point somewhere else. There is no third mechanism.
974	
975	**Where these hooks earn their keep in industry:**
976	
977	| Hook | Real job | Why there |
978	|---|---|---|
979	| `pre-commit` | run a formatter (`black`, `prettier`, `clang-format`) so the whole team's code looks identical | before the commit exists — nothing bad is recorded |
980	| `pre-commit` | **scan for secrets** — AWS keys, passwords, API tokens | once a key is committed and pushed, it is in the history forever; it must be stopped here |
981	| `pre-commit` | run the linter on staged files only — fast | keeps the check quick enough that people don't disable it |
982	| `commit-msg` | require a ticket ID (`JIRA-123: ...`) or the `feat:`/`fix:` convention | the message is final at this point |
983	| `commit-msg` | reject a message under ~10 characters ("fix", "asdf", "wip") | cheap way to keep history readable |
984	| `pre-push` | run the test suite | slower checks belong here — you push far less often than you commit |
985	| `pre-receive` | **protected branches**: refuse a direct push to `main`, force everything through a pull request | server-side, so `--no-verify` cannot help |
986	| `pre-receive` | reject a force-push that would erase history, or a file over 100 MB | protects everyone, not just the careful people |
987	| `post-receive` | start the CI build, deploy the site, post to the team's Slack channel | runs only after the push is safely accepted |
988	
989	Notice the pattern: **cheap checks early and locally, expensive checks later, unskippable checks on the server.**
990	
991	**Takeaway to say out loud:** "Hooks aren't cloned, because cloning must never run a stranger's script."

1035	**Cover this until every answer is written down.**

1070	
1071	## One-page reference
1072	
1073	**The `.git` folder**
1074	
1075	| Entry | What it holds |
1076	|---|---|
1077	| `HEAD` | text: which branch you are on (`ref: refs/heads/main`) |
1078	| `config` | this repository's settings |
1079	| `index` | the staging area — appears at the first `git add` |
1080	| `objects/` | every version of every file, named by content hash |
1081	| `refs/heads/<name>` | one file per branch, holding one commit hash |
1082	| `logs/` | the reflog — a diary of every branch movement |
1083	| `hooks/` | scripts Git runs at fixed moments |
1084	| `info/exclude` | private, uncommitted ignore rules |
1085	
1086	**The three config levels** (later beats earlier)
1087	
1088	| Level | File | Set with |
1089	|---|---|---|
1090	| system | `/etc/gitconfig` | `git config --system` |
1091	| global | `~/.gitconfig` | `git config --global` |
1092	| local | `.git/config` | `git config` |
1093	
1094	**The three object types**
1095	
1096	| Type | Holds | Knows the file name? |
1097	|---|---|---|
1098	| blob | one file's contents | **no** |
1099	| tree | a folder listing: mode, type, hash, name | **yes** |
1100	| commit | one tree, parent(s), author, date, message | no |
1101	
1102	**Commands for looking inside**
1103	
1104	| Command | Does |
1105	|---|---|
1106	| `git hash-object <file>` | calculate a hash without storing anything |
1107	| `git cat-file -t <hash>` | the object's type |
1108	| `git cat-file -p <hash>` | the object's contents, readable |
1109	| `git cat-file -s <hash>` | its size in bytes |
1110	| `git rev-parse HEAD` | the hash `HEAD` leads to |
1111	| `git ls-files -s` | what is in the index |
1112	| `git count-objects` | how many loose objects exist |
1113	
1114	**Hooks — when they fire and whether they can block**
1115	
1116	| Hook | Where | Fires | Blocks? |
1117	|---|---|---|---|
1118	| `pre-commit` | client | before the message is asked for | yes |
1119	| `prepare-commit-msg` | client | before you edit the message | yes |
1120	| `commit-msg` | client | message is final (path in `$1`) | yes |
1121	| `post-commit` | client | commit already made | no |
1122	| `pre-push` | client | before anything is sent | yes |
1123	| `pre-receive` | **server** | before any ref is updated | yes |
1124	| `update` | **server** | once per ref being updated | yes |
1125	| `post-receive` | **server** | after the push is accepted | no |
1126	
1127	**Rules to keep:**
1128	- `.git` is a folder of ordinary files; delete it and the history is gone.
1129	- The hash comes from the content — same content, same hash, everywhere.
1130	- `git add` writes the blob; `git commit` writes the tree and the commit.
1131	- Unchanged files are stored once, not once per commit.
1132	- A branch is a small file holding one hash.
1133	- A hook needs the **exact name** and `chmod +x`. `exit 0` allows, non-zero blocks.
1134	- Client hooks can be skipped with `--no-verify`; server hooks cannot.
1135	- Hooks are never cloned — they live in `.git/`.
1136	
1137	---

1142	|---|---|---|

## Task 22 — Pull Requests: What Is Actually Happening

- **Base filename:** `pull_requests` → `pull_requests_reference.md` (+ `_questions.md`, `_answers.md`)
- **Group in `tasks.html`:** `#tools`, after Task 21
- **Kind:** explanatory reading, not an iteration worksheet. No "a. What we set up / b. Task / c. Observation" — there is nothing for the student to set up. Sections instead, each ending with a one-line **"Say it out loud"** so it keeps the worksheet voice.
- **Audience assumption stated up front:** *you already know how to open a PR, review one and merge it. This page explains what Git and the website are doing while you click.*
- **Commands and transcripts appear only as illustrations** — shown with their real output to make a point, never as "now run this".
- **Leans on task 21 throughout:** commits are objects, a branch is a small file holding one hash, `pre-receive` is what a protected branch really is.

**Golden rule blockquote (draft):**
> A pull request is **not a Git command** — type `git pull-request` and Git will tell you no such thing exists. A PR is a *record kept by a website* saying: "branch X would like to go into branch Y." The commits are already on the server before the PR exists. Underneath every PR, however long the discussion, there is only ever **two branch names and one merge.**

### Sections

| # | Section | What it explains |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | A PR is not a Git thing | Git ships no PR. `git push` put the objects there; the PR is a row in GitHub's database naming two refs. Opening or closing a PR adds nothing to `.git/objects` and changes no branch. Why forges invented it |
| **2** | The four names in every PR | **base** ← **compare**, and the **merge base** — the newest commit both share. ASCII graph showing all four. Everything else follows from these |
| **3** | What "Files changed" is really showing | Two-dot `main..feature` vs three-dot `main...feature`. GitHub shows the **three-dot** diff: *what merging would change*, not *how the branches differ*. Worked example where they disagree, and why that surprises people |
| **4** | Why the PR updates itself when you push | A PR stores a **ref name**, not a snapshot. Push to the same branch → the PR silently becomes the new commits. Why "just push a fix" is the answer to review feedback, and why force-pushing a PR branch rewrites what reviewers already read |
| **5** | Review as a state machine | Comment / Approve / Request changes; single comments vs a submitted review; resolved conversations; suggestions as commits. Which of these actually blocks the merge and which is only social |
| **6** | The gate: why the button is grey | The full list — conflicts, required checks red or pending, not enough approvals, outstanding "request changes", branch behind base, unresolved conversations, CODEOWNERS not signed off. Each one mapped to the rule that produces it |
| **7** | **The three merge buttons, drawn** | Merge commit / Squash and merge / Rebase and merge, each with a before-and-after ASCII commit graph. What survives: two parents vs one new commit vs replayed commits with **new hashes**. Why the resulting file tree is identical in all three but the history is not. When each is the right choice |
| **8** | Conflicts | Why they happen (the base moved, not "you did something wrong"), why the **author** resolves them, merge-main-in vs rebase-onto-main and what each does to the PR, the `<<<<<<<` markers, and why a conflict is a fact about *lines* not about *correctness* |
| **9** | Protected branches, and what the merge button is allowed to do | Ties straight to task 21 iteration 8: protection is a `pre-receive` hook. `--no-verify` cannot help. The merge button works because the **server** performs the merge under its own rules, after the gate passed |
| **10** | After the merge | Where the commits end up, deleting the branch (and that the commits survive it), what `Closes #12` does, reverting a merged PR, and the difference between **closed** and **merged** |
| **11** | Fork-based PRs | `origin` vs `upstream`, a PR across two repositories, why open-source projects work this way, "allow edits by maintainers", keeping a fork current |
| **12** | Why teams work this way | One idea per PR, small diffs, the description explains *why* not *what*, draft PRs, linked issues, required reviewers, CI. The trade the whole ritual is buying |

Then, as always: **one-page reference** (anatomy of a PR · two-dot vs three-dot · the three strategies side by side · the grey-button checklist · PR states · `origin`/`upstream` · rules to keep), and last, the **New Words (కొత్త పదాలు)** Telugu table.

- **Part A** — 14 MCQ · **Part B** — 10 fill-in-the-blanks · **Part C** — 8 scenarios · **Part D** — read a commit graph and say which merge strategy produced it / what merging next would do.
- Answers mirror the numbering, every one with reasoning, closing "pattern to notice".

input.content:
# Pull Requests — What Is Actually Happening

**This page is different from the other tasks.** There is nothing to set up and nothing to run. You already know how to open a pull request, leave a review and merge it — you have done it. This page explains **what Git and the website are doing while you click**, so that when something behaves strangely you know why.

Read it once from top to bottom. After that, keep it as a reference: the one-page summary at the end has the tables you will actually come back for.

**Assumed:** Task 21 (Git Internals). Everything here leans on three facts from that task — a commit is an object named by a hash of its contents, a branch is a small text file holding one such hash, and a "protected branch" is a `pre-receive` hook on the server saying no.

**Commands in this page are illustrations, not instructions.** They are shown with their real output to make a point. You are not expected to run them, though nothing stops you.

> **The golden rule of pull requests**
> A pull request is **not a Git command.** Type `git pull-request` and Git will tell you no such thing exists. A PR is a *record kept by a website*, saying: "branch X would like to go into branch Y." The commits are already on the server **before** the PR exists. Underneath every PR — however long the discussion, however many reviewers — there is only ever **two branch names and one merge.**

*(A note on the examples: two people share one repository. **Asha** writes a change; **Ravi** reviews it. The commit hashes shown are from a real run — yours would be different, for the reason Task 21 gave: a commit contains its author and its timestamp.)*

---

## 1. A pull request is not a Git thing

Git does not have pull requests. Not in any version, not with any flag:

```
$ git pull-request
git: 'pull-request' is not a git command. See 'git --help'.
```

The whole idea belongs to the **forge** — the website hosting your repository: GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, Bitbucket. Git provides commits, branches and merging. The forge adds a place to *talk about a merge before it happens*.

So what exists on the server when a PR is open? Exactly this — and nothing more:

```
$ git ls-remote origin
11a9d5f5d2ed6f35624137bbfdc8eedc3d50e155	HEAD
b17cc20f028d01533aab78433ea5e787c2f70fb5	refs/heads/feature/greet
11a9d5f5d2ed6f35624137bbfdc8eedc3d50e155	refs/heads/main
```

Two branches. That is the entire Git-side content of the pull request. Asha's commits arrived on the server when she ran `git push`; the PR did not carry them there. Opening the PR:

- creates **no** new object in `.git/objects/`,
- moves **no** branch,
- changes **nothing** in the repository at all.

It writes a row in GitHub's own database: *PR #7, base `main`, compare `feature/greet`, state open, author Asha.* That is why opening and closing a PR is instant, and why you can close one and open it again with no effect on your code.

This also explains a thing that confuses people: **the PR is not a copy of your work.** If someone deletes the `feature/greet` branch from the server, the pull request has nothing left to show.

**Say it out loud:** "The push moves the commits. The pull request is just a note asking someone to merge them."

---

## 2. The four names in every pull request

Every PR is built from four things. Two you choose, one Git works out, one follows from the other three.

| Name | What it is | Who decides |
|---|---|---|
| **base** | the branch you want your work to end up in (usually `main`) | you, when you open the PR |
| **compare** | the branch holding your work (`feature/greet`) | you, when you open the PR |
| **merge base** | the newest commit that **both** branches already have | Git works it out |
| **the diff** | what would change if the merge happened | follows from the other three |

Here is the situation, drawn. Asha branched off `main`, made two commits, and while she was working Ravi pushed one commit to `main`:

```
                    A1 ──── A2        ← feature/greet   (compare)
                   ╱
      ──── M1 ────┘
             ╲
              ──── M2                 ← main            (base)

      M1 = the merge base: the newest commit both branches have
```

Git will tell you which commit that is:

```
$ git merge-base origin/main feature/greet
d5e5b26c485e17457c88b19beec10a4b7bc2216c
```

`d5e5b26` is `M1`, the "Initial project" commit — the last point where the two branches agreed. Everything the PR is about happened after it.

The commit list on the PR's **Commits** tab is exactly the commits on compare that are not on base:

```
$ git log --oneline origin/main..feature/greet
b17cc20 Greet a name
8aa453f Move greeting into a function
```

Two commits, which is what the PR will say: *"Asha wants to merge 2 commits into `main` from `feature/greet`."* Now you can read that sentence properly — it names the compare branch, the base branch, and the count from the command above.

**Say it out loud:** "Base, compare, and the merge base where they last agreed — everything else in the PR follows from those three."

---

## 3. What "Files changed" is really showing

This is the single most misunderstood thing about pull requests, and it is worth getting right, because sooner or later it will confuse you.

There are two ways to compare two branches, and they give **different answers**.

### Two dots — "how do these two branches differ?"

```
$ git diff origin/main..feature/greet
diff --git a/README.md b/README.md
index 1ebefdc..dfb4b07 100644
--- a/README.md
+++ b/README.md
@@ -1,3 +1 @@
 Team notes
-
-Build with: clang greet.c -o greet
diff --git a/greet.c b/greet.c
index d783c35..017fe55 100644
--- a/greet.c
+++ b/greet.c
@@ -1,6 +1,11 @@
 #include <stdio.h>
 
+void greet(const char *name)
+{
+    printf("Hello, %s\n", name);
+}
+
 int main(void)
 {
-    printf("Hello\n");
+    greet("world");
 }
```

Look at the first file. This says Asha's PR **deletes two lines from `README.md`** — the build instructions Ravi added.

**It does no such thing.** Asha never touched `README.md`. She has never even seen those lines; they were added to `main` after she branched off.

Why does the diff claim it? Because two dots compares the **tip of `main`** with the **tip of `feature/greet`**, as two piles of files. `main`'s pile has the build line; Asha's pile does not. Read as a change, "present on the left, absent on the right" means deletion. The comparison is honest — it is the question that was wrong.

### Three dots — "what would merging change?"

```
$ git diff origin/main...feature/greet
diff --git a/greet.c b/greet.c
index d783c35..017fe55 100644
--- a/greet.c
+++ b/greet.c
@@ -1,6 +1,11 @@
 #include <stdio.h>
 
+void greet(const char *name)
+{
+    printf("Hello, %s\n", name);
+}
+
 int main(void)
 {
-    printf("Hello\n");
+    greet("world");
 }
```

`README.md` is gone from the output. Only `greet.c` remains — which is the truth about what Asha did.

Three dots compares the **merge base** with the tip of compare. Not `M2...A2`, but `M1...A2`. It answers "what has Asha added since the branches parted?", and Ravi's README change is simply not part of that story.

Side by side:

```
$ git diff --stat origin/main..feature/greet      ← two dots
 README.md | 2 --
 greet.c   | 7 ++++++-
 2 files changed, 6 insertions(+), 3 deletions(-)

$ git diff --stat origin/main...feature/greet     ← three dots
 greet.c | 7 ++++++-
 1 file changed, 6 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)
```

**GitHub's "Files changed" tab is the three-dot diff.** So is the "+6 −1" badge, and so is the file count. This is why a PR that has been open for two weeks, while thirty other PRs merged into `main`, still shows only *your* files. It is comparing against the merge base, not against today's `main`.

| | Compares | Answers | Where you see it |
|---|---|---|---|
| `A..B` (two dots) | tip of A ↔ tip of B | "how do these two branches differ?" | almost never what you want for a PR |
| `A...B` (three dots) | **merge base** ↔ tip of B | "what does B add?" | **the PR's Files changed tab** |

One caution, and it is the reason the two-dot form exists at all: the three-dot diff shows what your branch *adds*, which is not quite the same as what the code will *look like* after the merge. If someone else edited a different part of the same file, the merged result contains both changes — but your PR's diff will never show you theirs. Section 8 is about what happens when those two changes collide.

**Say it out loud:** "Files changed is a three-dot diff — measured from where the branches parted, not from today's main."

---

## 4. Why the pull request updates itself when you push

Ravi reviews the PR and asks for a change. Asha does not open a new pull request. She commits a fix and pushes it to the same branch — and the existing PR quietly becomes the new version, with the review comments still attached.

This surprises people, and the reason is in Section 1. The PR's database row does not store commits. It stores a **branch name**. So:

```
PR #7:  base = main   compare = feature/greet
```

Whatever `refs/heads/feature/greet` points to *right now* is what the PR shows. Push a third commit and the branch file on the server holds a new hash; the PR redraws itself around it. Nothing needed updating, because nothing was ever copied.

Three consequences worth knowing:

**Pushing is how you answer a review.** There is no "submit new version" button because there is no version to submit. Push to the branch and you are done.

**Everything on that branch is in the PR, wanted or not.** A commit you pushed for an unrelated reason is now part of the proposal. This is the usual cause of "why are there 40 files in my PR" — the branch was made from the wrong starting point, so the merge base is far further back than intended.

**A force-push rewrites what the reviewer already read.** If you rebase or amend and then `git push --force`, the old commits are gone from the branch and the review comments were attached to lines in *those* commits. GitHub will mark them "outdated" and hide them, and Ravi has to read the whole thing again. Nothing is corrupted, but it is rude in a large review. `--force-with-lease` at least refuses to clobber work you have not seen; the politeness problem remains.

**Say it out loud:** "The PR follows a branch name, so pushing to the branch *is* updating the PR."

---

## 5. Review is a state machine

The Conversation tab looks like a chat, but underneath there are only a few distinct things, and only some of them affect whether the merge can happen.

| What you do | What it is | Blocks the merge? |
|---|---|---|
| Single line comment | one remark, posted immediately | no |
| **Review: Comment** | a bundle of remarks, no verdict | no |
| **Review: Approve** | a bundle plus "this is fine by me" | it *un*blocks — it is what a required approval counts |
| **Review: Request changes** | a bundle plus "not yet" | **yes**, until the same person approves or dismisses it |
| Suggestion | a comment containing replacement lines the author can commit with one click | no |
| Resolve conversation | marks a thread dealt with | only if the repo requires all conversations resolved |

Two things follow that are worth being clear about.

**"Request changes" is a lock held by one person.** It stays until *that reviewer* approves, or somebody with permission dismisses their review. Pushing a fix does not clear it — the fix is not automatically an answer, and only the reviewer can say whether it was. This is the usual reason a PR sits with a grey button while everybody assumes somebody else is blocking it.

**A single comment is not a review.** Remarks written in the diff and left as individual comments are sent one at a time and carry no verdict. Grouping them into a review, then choosing Approve or Request changes, is what makes the outcome visible to the gate in Section 6. A reviewer who writes ten comments and never submits a review has, formally, not reviewed anything.

**Say it out loud:** "Only Approve and Request changes move the gate. Everything else is conversation."

---

## 6. The gate: why the merge button is grey

The button has one job: tell you whether every rule this repository was configured with is currently satisfied. When it is grey, exactly one of these is false.

| Condition | What it means | Who set it |
|---|---|---|
| **No conflicts with base** | Git can combine the two sides without a human choosing | always required — this one is Git, not policy |
| **Required checks passed** | CI finished and every required job is green | repo settings |
| **Enough approvals** | e.g. at least 1, or 2 | repo settings |
| **No outstanding "request changes"** | nobody is still holding the lock from Section 5 | repo settings |
| **Conversations resolved** | every review thread marked resolved | repo settings, optional |
| **CODEOWNERS approved** | the owner of a touched path has approved | the `CODEOWNERS` file |
| **Branch up to date with base** | compare contains the latest base commit | repo settings, optional |
| **You have permission to merge** | write access, or maintainer on the repo | repo settings |

Only the first is a fact about Git. **Everything else is policy** — a switch someone turned on. This is why the same PR would merge instantly in one repository and sit blocked for a day in another; the code is identical, the rules are not.

Two of these are worth a closer look.

**Checks are just programs.** A "check" is some machine, somewhere, that noticed your push, ran a command, and reported back pass or fail. Nothing more mysterious. It is `pre-push` from Task 21 moved onto a server that never gets tired and cannot be skipped with `--no-verify`. A **pending** check is not a failing check — nothing has reported yet, and the button is grey for lack of an answer rather than because of a bad one.

**"Branch is out of date"** — the strictest setting, and the one people find most annoying. It insists your compare branch already contains the tip of base *before* you merge, so the tests that passed were run on the actual combination that is about to land. Without it a green PR can still break `main`: your change passed, their change passed, and the two together do not. That is called a **semantic conflict** — nothing overlaps textually, so Git is perfectly happy, and the build fails anyway. Section 3's warning about the three-dot diff is the same fact seen from the other side.

**Say it out loud:** "Only 'no conflicts' is Git. Every other grey button is a rule someone chose."

---

## 7. The three merge buttons, drawn

When the gate opens, GitHub offers up to three ways to land the work. They are not styles of the same operation — they produce **genuinely different histories**. The repository's settings decide which are available.

For all three, the starting point is the picture from Section 2:

```
                    8aa453f ──── b17cc20      ← feature/greet
                   ╱
      ──── d5e5b26┘
             ╲
              ──── 11a9d5f                    ← main
```

### Create a merge commit

```
$ git log --oneline --graph --all
*   9aab251 Merge pull request #7 from asha/feature/greet
|\
| * b17cc20 Greet a name
| * 8aa453f Move greeting into a function
* | 11a9d5f Document the build command
|/
* d5e5b26 Initial project
```

A new commit is created with **two parents** — one on each side:

```
$ git cat-file -p main
tree b53b12e6c5218ff58a8502176e904308d4bcea5f
parent 11a9d5f5d2ed6f35624137bbfdc8eedc3d50e155     ← old main
parent b17cc20f028d01533aab78433ea5e787c2f70fb5     ← the PR branch
```

Two `parent` lines. Task 21 showed a commit with one; this is what a merge commit is, and it is the only kind of commit that has more than one. Asha's original commits survive untouched, with their original hashes. The history now records that a branch existed and when it came back.

### Squash and merge

```
* 4529aba Greet a name (#7)
* 11a9d5f Document the build command
* d5e5b26 Initial project
```

All the branch's commits are flattened into **one new commit** on `main`, with a single parent. `8aa453f` and `b17cc20` are not in `main`'s history at all — the new `4529aba` contains their combined effect under a new hash. `main` becomes a straight line, one commit per PR.

The original commits still exist as objects while the branch exists, but once the branch is deleted nothing points at them and they are eventually cleaned up.

### Rebase and merge

```
* 6f523d7 Greet a name
* c6fd0b9 Move greeting into a function
* 11a9d5f Document the build command
* d5e5b26 Initial project
```

Each commit is **replayed** on top of `main`, one at a time. You keep the separate commits *and* get a straight line — but look at the hashes. `8aa453f` became `c6fd0b9`, and `b17cc20` became `6f523d7`. Different parent, therefore different commit content, therefore different hash. Task 21's rule again: the hash comes from the contents, and a commit's contents include its parent.

**These are not the same commits moved. They are new commits with the same changes.**

### The fact that ties it together

```
merge commit  → tree b53b12e6c5218ff58a8502176e904308d4bcea5f
squash        → tree b53b12e6c5218ff58a8502176e904308d4bcea5f
rebase        → tree b53b12e6c5218ff58a8502176e904308d4bcea5f
```

**All three produce exactly the same tree.** Identical files, byte for byte. Check out `main` after any of the three and you cannot tell which button was pressed by looking at the code — only by looking at the history.

So the choice is never about the result. It is entirely about what you want the log to say afterwards:

| | History shape | Original commits | Good when |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Merge commit** | branching, honest | kept, same hashes | you want the true record; large or long-running work |
| **Squash** | one straight line | replaced by one | PRs are one small idea; messy "wip", "fix typo" commits you do not want kept |
| **Rebase** | straight line, several commits | replayed, **new hashes** | the individual commits are each worth keeping, but you dislike merge bubbles |

One warning about rebase and squash. Both **rewrite** the commits, so anybody who had that branch checked out now has commits that no longer exist anywhere. Harmless for a PR branch about to be deleted; painful if a colleague built work on top of it.

**Say it out loud:** "All three give the same files. They differ only in what the history remembers."

---

## 8. Conflicts

A conflict means: **both sides changed the same lines, and Git will not guess.** It is not an error, not a sign anybody did anything wrong, and not a comment on whether the code is correct.

Asha's branch changed the greeting to `"Hello, world\n"`. While her PR was open, a different PR changing the same line to `"Namaste\n"` was merged into `main`:

```
* 41963b6 Say Namaste          ← main
| * 995fa62 Greet the world    ← feature/greet
|/
* 1189799 Initial project
```

The same line of the same file, changed two different ways since the merge base. Git can pair up changes to *different* lines by itself; it cannot pick between two rewrites of *one* line, because both are valid and only a person knows which is meant.

**The author resolves it, not the reviewer.** Not out of politeness — the reviewer usually cannot. The fix has to be committed onto the compare branch, and only someone who can push to that branch can do it. (This is what "allow edits by maintainers" in Section 11 is for.)

Asha brings `main` into her branch:

```
$ git merge origin/main
Auto-merging greet.c
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in greet.c
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
```

Git writes both versions into the file and stops:

```
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
<<<<<<< HEAD
    printf("Hello, world\n");
=======
    printf("Namaste\n");
>>>>>>> origin/main
}
```

Three markers, and the middle one is the one people misread:

| Marker | Means |
|---|---|
| `<<<<<<< HEAD` | below this is **your branch's** version |
| `=======` | the divider — **not** part of anything, delete it |
| `>>>>>>> origin/main` | above this is the **incoming** version |

`git status` shows the file as `UU` — unmerged on both sides:

```
$ git status --short
UU greet.c
```

Resolving means editing the file until it says what you want, **markers removed**, then `git add` and commit. You are not obliged to pick a side; here the honest answer is neither of the two:

```
    printf("Namaste, world\n");
```

```
$ git add greet.c
$ git commit --no-edit
$ git log --oneline --graph --all
*   718ff74 Merge remote-tracking branch 'origin/main' into feature/greet
|\
| * 41963b6 Say Namaste
* | 995fa62 Greet the world
|/
* 1189799 Initial project
```

Push that, and the PR goes mergeable again. Notice what the PR's diff has become:

```
$ git diff origin/main...feature/greet
@@ -2,5 +2,5 @@

 int main(void)
 {
-    printf("Namaste\n");
+    printf("Namaste, world\n");
 }
```

The merge base moved forward to include `41963b6`, so the three-dot diff is now measured from there. Ravi's `Namaste` is part of the baseline rather than part of the proposal, and the PR correctly shows the only thing still being *proposed*: adding `, world`. **Resolving a conflict usually makes a PR's diff smaller.**

There are two ways to update a branch, and they leave different marks:

| | What it does | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Merge base into branch** (above) | adds a merge commit to your branch | an extra commit in the PR; safe, never rewrites anything |
| **Rebase branch onto base** | replays your commits on the new base | clean straight line, but new hashes → force-push → outdated review comments (Section 4) |

GitHub's "Update branch" button does the first. Its web conflict editor can resolve simple cases in the browser and commits the result to your branch — the same operation, done for you.

**Say it out loud:** "A conflict means two edits to one line. Git is not confused — it is refusing to guess."

---

## 9. Protected branches, and what the merge button is allowed to do

Task 21 ended with a server-side `pre-receive` hook refusing a push:

```
remote: [server] REJECTED: main is protected, open a pull request
 ! [remote rejected] main -> main (pre-receive hook declined)
```

That is all a protected branch is. GitHub's version is a settings page rather than a shell script, but it runs in the same place, at the same moment, and does the same thing: examine the incoming ref update and decline it.

Which answers a question worth asking. **If nobody can push to `main`, how does the merge button push to `main`?**

Because the merge does not happen on your machine at all. When you press it, the **server** performs the merge in its own copy and updates `refs/heads/main` itself — as the forge, under the rule "an approved pull request that passed the gate may update this branch". Your laptop sends one HTTPS request saying "merge PR #7". No push leaves your machine.

That is the whole design, and it is the reason two things you might have tried do not work:

- **`--no-verify` cannot help.** It skips *client* hooks — `pre-commit`, `commit-msg`, `pre-push` — which live on your machine and are yours to skip. Branch protection is server-side. Your flag never reaches it.
- **Neither can `--force`.** A force-push is still a push, and protection normally refuses those specifically.

The rule to carry away from both tasks: **a check you can skip is a helpful reminder; a check on the server is a rule.** Teams put the fast, friendly checks locally so mistakes are caught early, and put the ones that actually matter on the server, where good intentions are not required.

**Say it out loud:** "The merge button works because the server merges, not me — and the server is the thing enforcing the rule."

---

## 10. After the merge

**The commits are now on base.** Depending on the button, either the originals (merge), or one new commit (squash), or replayed copies (rebase). `main` moved; that is what merging is.

**Deleting the branch deletes nothing.** The prompt appears right after merging and it is safe to take. Remember Task 21: a branch is a small file holding one hash. Deleting it removes the file, not the commits — those are reachable from `main` now, which is the whole point. The PR page keeps working afterwards and its diff still renders.

**`Closes #12` in the description closes issue 12** — automatically, at the moment the PR merges, and only if the PR merged into the repository's default branch. It also links the two so each shows the other. `Fixes` and `Resolves` behave identically; a bare `#12` links without closing.

**Merged is not the same as closed.** A PR ends in one of two states, and the difference matters:

| End state | Means | Reopenable |
|---|---|---|
| **Merged** | the commits are on the base branch | no — it happened |
| **Closed** | abandoned; nothing was merged | yes, while the branch still exists |

A closed PR left no trace in the code. If the branch is then deleted, the work is genuinely gone from the server.

**Undoing a merged PR: revert, do not delete.** GitHub's Revert button opens a *new* PR containing a commit that applies the opposite changes. History is not rewritten — the original merge stays in the log, followed by its undo. That is deliberate: rewriting a shared `main` breaks the repository for everyone who has already pulled it. Two visible commits are the correct price.

**Say it out loud:** "Merged and closed are different endings. Undo by adding a revert, never by rewriting main."

---

## 11. Fork-based pull requests

So far both people could push to the same repository. But you can open a PR against a project where you have **no write access at all** — this is how essentially all open-source contribution works, and the mechanism is worth understanding.

A **fork** is your own copy of someone else's repository, on the server, under your account. You have full write access to your copy and none to theirs.

```
      github.com/aikaryashala/jun-2026     ← upstream (you cannot push)
                    │  fork
                    ▼
      github.com/asha/jun-2026             ← origin   (yours; push freely)
                    │  clone
                    ▼
      ~/jun-2026 on your VM
```

Cloning your fork gives you one remote. Most people add the second by hand:

```
$ git remote -v
origin      https://github.com/asha/jun-2026.git       (fetch)
origin      https://github.com/asha/jun-2026.git       (push)
upstream    https://github.com/aikaryashala/jun-2026.git (fetch)
upstream    https://github.com/aikaryashala/jun-2026.git (push)
```

The names are pure convention — Git attaches no meaning to either — but the convention is universal:

| Remote | Points at | You push to it? |
|---|---|---|
| `origin` | **your fork** | yes |
| `upstream` | the **original** repository | no |

The flow: branch, commit, push to `origin`, then open a PR whose compare is `asha:feature/greet` and whose base is `aikaryashala:main`. **A pull request can cross repositories** — the base and compare in Section 2 were both in one repository only because that was the simple case. Nothing else about the PR changes: same diff, same review, same gate, same buttons.

Two practical points.

**Your fork does not update itself.** It was a copy taken at one moment. Weeks later `upstream/main` has moved and yours has not, so branch from a stale point and your PR carries other people's already-merged work. The fix is to fetch upstream and fast-forward before starting:

```
git fetch upstream
git switch main
git merge --ff-only upstream/main
git push origin main
```

(GitHub's "Sync fork" button does exactly this.)

**"Allow edits by maintainers"** is the checkbox on the PR form that lets the project's maintainers push to your PR branch. Without it they can only ask you to fix things; with it they can rebase your branch or resolve a small conflict themselves. It is worth leaving on — and it grants access to that one branch, not to your fork.

**Say it out loud:** "`origin` is my fork and I push to it; `upstream` is theirs and I only ever read from it."

---

## 12. Why teams work this way

The ritual costs real time. What is it buying?

**Nothing reaches `main` that nobody else has seen.** That is the actual product. Every other benefit — the discussion, the checks, the record — follows from that one rule.

Things that make a PR easy to review, all of which follow from what the earlier sections showed:

- **One idea per PR.** Not "one file", not "one day's work" — one reason. Two unrelated changes should be two PRs, because a reviewer who disagrees with half of one PR cannot approve the other half.
- **Small.** A 50-line diff gets real comments. A 2,000-line diff gets "LGTM" and nobody learns anything.
- **The description explains *why*.** The diff already says what changed — the reviewer can read it. What they cannot read is what you were trying to do, what else you tried, and what you are unsure about. Write that.
- **Draft PRs are for work in progress.** Open one early to show direction or trigger the checks; it cannot be merged until you mark it ready, and reviewers know not to spend time yet.
- **Link the issue.** `Closes #12` gives the next person the context that no diff can carry.
- **Branch from current base and push early.** Both keep the merge base recent, which keeps conflicts small (Section 8) and the diff honest (Section 3).
- **Reply to every comment.** Even "done" or "kept it, because…". A thread left silent stalls the PR, and, per Section 5, only the reviewer can lift a Request changes.

And from the reviewer's side: review promptly, because an open PR ages badly — `main` moves under it, conflicts accumulate, and the author has moved on. Say clearly whether you are blocking or just remarking. Approve when it is good enough, not when it is what you would have written.

**Say it out loud:** "The whole ritual buys one thing: nothing lands on main that only one person has seen."

---

## One-page reference

**Anatomy of a pull request**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| base | the branch the work should end up in (`main`) |
| compare / head | the branch holding the work (`feature/greet`) |
| merge base | newest commit both branches share — `git merge-base A B` |
| the diff | merge base ↔ tip of compare (a **three-dot** diff) |
| draft | open, but explicitly not ready to merge |
| the PR itself | a row in the forge's database; **no** Git object |

**Two dots vs three dots**

| Form | Compares | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| `main..feature` | tip ↔ tip | how the two branches differ |
| `main...feature` | **merge base** ↔ tip of feature | what feature adds — **this is the PR's Files changed** |

**The three merge buttons**

| | Parents | Original commits | History |
|---|---|---|---|
| Merge commit | **two** | kept, same hashes | shows the branch |
| Squash and merge | one | replaced by one new commit | straight line, one commit per PR |
| Rebase and merge | one | replayed, **new hashes** | straight line, commits kept |

All three produce the **same tree** — identical files. Only the history differs.

**Why the button is grey**

- conflicts with base *(the only Git-level reason)*
- a required check is failing — or still pending
- not enough approvals
- someone's "Request changes" is unresolved
- unresolved conversations
- CODEOWNERS has not approved
- branch is behind base *(if that rule is on)*
- you lack permission to merge

**Review actions that move the gate:** Approve, Request changes. Nothing else.

**PR end states**

| State | Commits on base? | Reopenable |
|---|---|---|
| Merged | yes | no |
| Closed | no | yes, while the branch exists |

**Remotes, when forking**

| Remote | Repository | Push? |
|---|---|---|
| `origin` | your fork | yes |
| `upstream` | the original | no — fetch only |

**Conflict markers**

| Marker | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `<<<<<<< HEAD` | your branch's version starts |
| `=======` | divider — delete it |
| `>>>>>>> origin/main` | incoming version ends |

**Rules to keep:**
- Git has no pull request. The push moved the commits; the PR is a note.
- A PR stores a **branch name**, so pushing to the branch updates the PR.
- "Files changed" is measured from the **merge base**, not from today's base.
- Only "no conflicts" is Git. Every other grey button is a rule someone chose.
- All three merge buttons give identical files and different histories.
- A conflict means two edits to one line — the **author** resolves it.
- Branch protection is a server-side hook; `--no-verify` cannot reach it.
- The merge button works because the **server** does the merge.
- Deleting a merged branch deletes a file holding a hash, not your commits.
- Undo a merged PR with a revert, never by rewriting shared history.

---

## New Words (కొత్త పదాలు — తెలుగు అర్థాలు)

| English | తెలుగు | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| pull request (PR) | పుల్ రిక్వెస్ట్ | "నా బ్రాంచ్‌ని మీ బ్రాంచ్‌లో కలపండి" అనే అభ్యర్థన |
| forge | ఫోర్జ్ | రిపోను హోస్ట్ చేసే వెబ్‌సైట్ (GitHub, GitLab) |
| base branch | బేస్ బ్రాంచ్ | పని చేరవలసిన బ్రాంచ్ (సాధారణంగా `main`) |
| compare branch | కంపేర్ బ్రాంచ్ | మీ పని ఉన్న బ్రాంచ్ |
| merge base | మెర్జ్ బేస్ | రెండు బ్రాంచ్‌లకూ ఉమ్మడిగా ఉన్న చివరి కమిట్ |
| diff | డిఫ్ | ఏమి మారిందో చూపే జాబితా |
| review | రివ్యూ | మరొకరు మీ కోడ్‌ను పరిశీలించడం |
| approve | అప్రూవ్ | "ఇది సరిగ్గా ఉంది" అని రివ్యూయర్ చెప్పడం |
| request changes | రిక్వెస్ట్ ఛేంజెస్ | "ఇంకా కాదు — మార్చండి" — మెర్జ్‌ను ఆపుతుంది |
| merge commit | మెర్జ్ కమిట్ | రెండు పేరెంట్‌లు ఉన్న ఏకైక రకం కమిట్ |
| squash | స్క్వాష్ | అన్ని కమిట్‌లను ఒక్క కమిట్‌గా చేయడం |
| rebase | రీబేస్ | కమిట్‌లను కొత్త బేస్ మీద మళ్ళీ ఆడించడం — కొత్త హాష్‌లు |

| protected branch | రక్షిత బ్రాంచ్ | నేరుగా పుష్ చేయనివ్వని బ్రాంచ్ |
